passages.t: Marriage and food are God's good gifts
passages.happening:
“Now the Spirit expressly states that in later times some will abandon the faith to follow deceitful spirits and the teachings of demons, influenced by the hypocrisy of liars, whose consciences are seared with a hot iron” (verses 1-2).

“They will prohibit marriage and require abstinence from certain foods that God has created to be received with thanksgiving by those who believe and know the truth. For every creation of God is good, and nothing that is received with thanksgiving should be rejected, because it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer” (verses 3-5).
passages.hearers:
‘Later times’ does not mean some far-off future. The New Testament sees the whole time between Christ's first coming and his return as the last days. Jesus had warned that false teachers would come (Mark 13:22), and Paul had warned the Ephesian elders (Acts 20:29-30). Now it was happening in Ephesus.

The false teachers looked very spiritual. They said no to marriage and no to certain foods. In that world several ideas could lead there. Some Greek thinkers treated the body and matter as lower than the soul, so that saying no to bodily pleasure seemed holy. Some Jewish groups kept strict rules about food, and ancient writers say some Essenes did not marry. And some false teachers may have thought the resurrection had already happened (2 Timothy 2:18), so that believers should already live like the angels, who do not marry.

Paul's answer goes back to creation. ‘Every creation of God is good.’ Marriage and food are not traps. They are gifts. And the right way to receive a gift is with thanks. Food received ‘with thanksgiving’ is ‘sanctified’, set apart for God's use, by God's word and by prayer. That is one reason Christians give thanks before meals.

Notice how strongly Paul speaks. A teaching that despises God's good gifts is not a higher spirituality. It is a lie, however holy it looks. ‘Seared with a hot iron’ means a conscience so burned that it no longer feels anything.
passages.ot:
The first page of the Bible says it: “And God looked upon all that He had made, and indeed, it was very good” (Genesis 1:31).

Marriage was God's gift from the beginning: “For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and they will become one flesh” (Genesis 2:24). “He who finds a wife finds a good thing and obtains favor from the LORD” (Proverbs 18:22).

And food is God's gift too: “The eyes of all look to You, and You give them their food in season” (Psalm 145:15). After the flood God said to Noah, “just as I gave you the green plants, I now give you all things” (Genesis 9:3).
passages.hard:
Does this mean it is wrong for a Christian not to marry, or to fast, or to keep away from some foods?

No. Paul's target is teachers who forbade marriage and foods as a rule for everyone, as if God's gifts were unclean and holiness meant refusing them. He himself was unmarried and said that singleness can be a gift (1 Corinthians 7:7). Jesus fasted, and taught his followers how to fast (Matthew 6:16-18). Many Christians choose not to eat certain things, or not to drink, for their health or their conscience or the sake of others, and Paul elsewhere asks believers to respect one another in such choices (Romans 14).

What Paul rejects is the claim that marriage, food or the body is bad in itself, or that saying no to them makes someone more spiritual than other believers. The body is God's good creation, and it will be raised. Nothing here pressures anyone to marry, and nothing here shames anyone who is single.
passages.asks: Paul says that everything God made is good, to be received with thanks. Ask whether you receive your food, your body and your relationships as gifts or as problems. Ask whether you give thanks before you eat, and mean it. And ask whether you have ever looked down on other believers for enjoying good things you give up.

passages.happening:
“By pointing out these things to the brothers, you will be a good servant of Christ Jesus, nourished by the words of faith and sound instruction that you have followed. But reject irreverent, silly myths. Instead, train yourself for godliness” (verses 6-7).

“For physical exercise is of limited value, but godliness is valuable in every way, holding promise for the present life and for the one to come. This is a trustworthy saying, worthy of full acceptance” (verses 8-9).

“To this end we labor and strive, because we have set our hope on the living God, who is the Savior of everyone, and especially of those who believe” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Paul tells Timothy to be ‘nourished’, fed, on the words of the faith. A teacher has to eat before he can feed others.

Then comes a picture every reader in Ephesus knew. Greek cities had a gymnasium, a central place where young men exercised, bathed and were taught. The Greek word for ‘train’ is the word from which ‘gymnasium’ comes. Paul does not mock physical exercise. He says it has some value. But godliness is worth more, because it pays off now and for ever.

Godliness means reverence for God, lived out in ordinary life. Paul says you train for it the way an athlete trains: on purpose, with effort, day after day. It does not happen by accident.

The false teachers had their own training: rules about food and marriage. Paul's training is different. It is not about refusing God's gifts. It is about growing in love, faith and purity.

Then verse 10. ‘We labor and strive.’ Paul's work was hard. But he kept going because his hope was set ‘on the living God, who is the Savior of everyone, and especially of those who believe’. That phrase has been read in more than one way, as the part below sets out.
passages.ot:
The law was meant to nourish God's people: “But his delight is in the Law of the LORD, and on His law he meditates day and night” (Psalm 1:2). “Hold on to instruction; do not let go. Guard it, for it is your life” (Proverbs 4:13).

God's care for all he has made is the song of the Psalms: “The LORD is good to all; His compassion rests on all He has made” (Psalm 145:9). “O LORD, You preserve man and beast” (Psalm 36:6).

And God as the only Saviour is Isaiah's message: “I, yes I, am the LORD, and there is no Savior but Me” (Isaiah 43:11).
passages.hard:
If God is ‘the Savior of everyone’, will everyone be saved?

The phrase has been read in several ways. The most common reading takes ‘Savior’ in two senses. God preserves and cares for all people in his general kindness, and the Greek word for saviour was used widely of anyone who protected or provided for others; and he saves those who believe in the full sense, for eternal life. A second reading holds that God is the Saviour offered to all, whose salvation becomes real for those who believe. A third notes that the word translated ‘especially’ can sometimes mean ‘that is’, so that God is the Saviour of all people, namely those who believe. Some Christian universalists have read the verse as teaching that all people will finally be saved.

Most readers across the traditions do not read it that way here, because the verse itself sets believers apart, and because the same letter warns that some have ‘shipwrecked their faith’ (1:19) and speaks of ‘ruin and destruction’ (6:9). These notes do not choose among the readings. What the verse plainly says, with 2:4, is that God's saving care is wide, and that faith matters.
passages.asks: Paul tells Timothy to train for godliness the way an athlete trains. Ask what you are training yourself in each day: habits that grow reverence for God, or habits that crowd him out. Ask what you are feeding on. And ask where your hope is set when your work for God is hard.

passages.t: Let no one despise your youth
passages.happening:
“Command and teach these things. Let no one despise your youth, but set an example for the believers in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity. Until I come, devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation, and to teaching” (verses 11-13).

“Do not neglect the gift that is in you, which was given you through the prophecy spoken over you at the laying on of the hands of the elders” (verse 14). “Pay close attention to your life and to your teaching. Persevere in these things, for by so doing you will save both yourself and those who hear you” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
Timothy was young, at least by the standards of his world, where ‘youth’ could describe a man well into his thirties and respect usually followed age. He was correcting older men, some of them teachers. They might well look down on him.

Paul's answer is not to tell him to demand respect. It is to earn it: ‘set an example’ in five things. Speech and conduct, what he says and does. Love, faith and purity, what he is inside. A young leader whose life is clean is hard to dismiss.

Then three tasks for the church's gatherings. The ‘public reading of Scripture’ came from the synagogue, where the law and the prophets were read aloud each Sabbath. Few people owned a copy of the Scriptures, which were written by hand and costly, so most believers knew the Bible by hearing it. After the reading came ‘exhortation’, urging people to live it, and ‘teaching’, explaining what it means.

Timothy had been set apart for his work when the elders laid their hands on him, and words had been spoken over him (see 1:18). Paul tells him not to let that gift go cold.

And verse 16 holds the whole letter together: ‘your life and your teaching’. Watch both. A sound teacher with a careless life, or a good life with false teaching, will not do. ‘You will save both yourself and those who hear you’ does not mean Timothy saves anyone by his own power. It means that by holding on to the truth and living it, he will keep himself and his hearers in the way of salvation.
passages.ot:
God called Jeremiah when he was young and afraid: “Ah, Lord GOD,” I said, “I surely do not know how to speak, for I am only a child!” And God answered, “Do not say, ‘I am only a child.’ For to everyone I send you, you must go” (Jeremiah 1:6-7). A psalm asks, “How can a young man keep his way pure? By guarding it according to Your word” (Psalm 119:9).

The public reading of Scripture goes back to the law: “you are to read this law in the hearing of all Israel” (Deuteronomy 31:11). When Ezra read it, the leaders were “explaining it and giving insight, so that the people could understand what was being read” (Nehemiah 8:8).

And the laying on of hands for a task began with Moses: “Take Joshua son of Nun, a man with the Spirit in him, and lay your hands on him” (Numbers 27:18).
passages.asks: Paul tells a young leader to earn respect by his example, and to watch both his life and his teaching. Ask whether your life backs up what you say about God. Ask which of the five, speech, conduct, love, faith or purity, needs the most attention in you. And if you are young, ask how you could set an example for older believers, not by demanding respect but by earning it.
